questions.knowledge_point: Finding the Total Displacement of a Particle Given Its Velocity
questions.worked_solution:
We find the total displacement by calculating the definite integral of the velocity.

Let $d$ be the total displacement between $t=0$ and $t=5.$ Then we have

$$
\begin{aligned}d & ={\int }_{0}^{5}(6{t}^{2}-4t)\,\text{dt} \\  & =(2{t}^{3}-2{t}^{2}){|}_{0}^{5} \\  & =[2(5)^{3}-2(5)^{2}]-[2(0)^{3}-2(0)^{2}] \\  & =[250-50]-0 \\  & =200.\end{aligned}
$$

We find the total displacement by calculating the definite integral of the velocity.

Let $d$ be the total displacement. Then we have

$$
\begin{aligned}d & ={\int }_{1}^{4}(6{t}^{2}-2t)\,\text{d}t \\  & =(2{t}^{3}-{t}^{2}){|}_{1}^{4} \\  & =[2(4)^{3}-(4)^{2}]-[2(1)^{3}-(1)^{2}] \\  & =[128-16]-[2-1] \\  & =112-1 \\  & =111.\end{aligned}
$$

So the total displacement between $t=1$ and $t=4$ is $111.$

questions.knowledge_point: Finding the Final Position of a Particle
questions.problem: A particle $P$ moves along the $x$-axis and its velocity at time $t>0$ is given by $v(t)=6{t}^{2}+4t.$ At time $t=4$ the particle is located at the position $x=-300.$ What is the position of the particle at time $t=7?$
questions.worked_solution:
The position of the particle at $t=7$ is equal to its position at $t=4$ plus the total displacement over $t\in [4,7].$ Therefore, we can calculate it as follows:

$$
x(7)=x(4)+{\int }_{4}^{7}v(t)\,\text{d}t
$$

Carrying out the computations, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}x(7) & =-300+{\int }_{4}^{7}(6{t}^{2}+4t)\,\text{dt} \\  & =-300+{[2{t}^{3}+2{t}^{2})]}_{4}^{7} \\  & =-300+([2(7)^{3}+2(7)^{2}]-[2(4)^{3}+2(4)^{2}]) \\  & =-300+([686+98]-[128+32]) \\  & =-300+(784-160) \\  & =-300+624 \\  & =324.\end{aligned}
$$

So the position of the particle at $t=7$ is $x=324.$

questions.knowledge_point: Finding the Final Position of a Particle
questions.problem:
A particle $Q$ moves along the $x$-axis and its velocity at time $t\ge 0$ is given by $v(t)=\operatorname{cos}⁡(t)-\operatorname{sin}⁡(t).$ At time $t=\frac{\pi }{2}$ the particle is located at the position $x=5.$ 
Find the position of the particle at time $t=\pi .$ Do not round the answer.

The position of the particle at $t=\pi $ is $x=$
{{field-1}}.
questions.worked_solution:
The position of the particle at $t=\pi $ is equal to its position at $t=\frac{\pi }{2}$ plus the total displacement over $t\in [\frac{\pi }{2},\pi ].$ Therefore, we can calculate it as follows:

$$
x(\pi )=x(\frac{\pi }{2})+{\int }_{\pi /2}^{\pi }v(t)\,\text{d}t
$$

Carrying out the computations, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}x(\pi ) & =5+{\int }_{\pi /2}^{\pi }(\operatorname{cos}⁡(t)-\operatorname{sin}⁡(t))\,\text{d}t \\  & =5+{[\operatorname{sin}⁡(t)+\operatorname{cos}⁡(t)]}_{\pi /2}^{\pi } \\  & =5+[\operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi )+\operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi )]-[\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi }{2})+\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\pi }{2})) \\  & =5+(0-1)-(1+0) \\  & =5-2 \\  & =3.\end{aligned}
$$

So, the position of the particle at $t=\pi $ is $x=3.$

questions.knowledge_point: Finding the Final Position of a Particle
questions.problem: A particle $P$ moves along the $x$-axis and its velocity at time $t\ge 0$ is given by $v(t)=\operatorname{sin}⁡(t-\frac{\pi }{3}).$ At time $t=\frac{\pi }{3}$ the particle is located at the position $x=\frac{1}{2}.$ What is the position of the particle at time $t=\pi ?$
questions.worked_solution:
The position of the particle at $t=\pi $ is equal to its position at $t=\frac{\pi }{3}$ plus the total displacement over $t\in [\frac{\pi }{3},\pi ].$ Therefore, we can calculate it as follows:

$$
x(\pi )=x(\frac{\pi }{3})+{\int }_{\pi /3}^{\pi }v(t)\,\text{d}t
$$

Carrying out the computations, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}x(\pi ) & =\frac{1}{2}+{\int }_{\pi /3}^{\pi }\operatorname{sin}⁡(t-\frac{\pi }{3})\,\text{d}t \\  & =\frac{1}{2}+{[-\operatorname{cos}⁡(t-\frac{\pi }{3})]}_{\pi /3}^{\pi } \\  & =\frac{1}{2}+([-\operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi -\frac{\pi }{3})]-[-\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\pi }{3}-\frac{\pi }{3})]) \\  & =\frac{1}{2}+(-\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{2\pi }{3})+\operatorname{cos}⁡(0)) \\  & =\frac{1}{2}+(-(-\frac{1}{2})+1) \\  & =\frac{1}{2}+\frac{1}{2}+1 \\  & =2.\end{aligned}
$$

So, the position of the particle at $t=\pi $ is $x=2.$

questions.problem: A particle $P$ moves along the $x$-axis and its velocity at time $t>0$ is given by $v(t)={e}^{t-1}.$ At time $t=1$ the particle is located at the position $x=2.$ What is the position of the particle at time $t=2?$
questions.worked_solution:
The position of the particle at $t=2$ is equal to its position at $t=1$ plus the total displacement over $t\in [1,2].$ Therefore, we can calculate it as follows:

$$
x(2)=x(1)+{\int }_{1}^{2}v(t)\,\text{d}t
$$

Carrying out the computations, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}x(2) & =2+{\int }_{1}^{2}{e}^{t-1}\,\text{d}t \\  & =2+{[{e}^{t-1}]}_{1}^{2} \\  & =2+({e}^{2-1}-{e}^{1-1}) \\  & =2+({e}^{1}-{e}^{0}) \\  & =2+e-1 \\  & =e+1.\end{aligned}
$$

So the position of the particle at $t=2$ is $x=e+1.$

The position of the particle at $t=5$ is equal to its position at $t=1$ plus the total displacement over $t\in [1,5].$ Therefore, we can calculate it as follows:

$$
x(5)=x(1)+{\int }_{1}^{5}v(t)\,\text{d}t
$$

Carrying out the computations, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}x(5) & =2{e}^{2}+{\int }_{1}^{5}3{e}^{3t-1}\,\text{d}t \\  & =2{e}^{2}+{[{e}^{3t-1}]}_{1}^{5} \\  & =2{e}^{2}+({e}^{3(5)-1}-{e}^{3(1)-1}) \\  & =2{e}^{2}+({e}^{14}-{e}^{2}) \\  & =2{e}^{2}+{e}^{14}-{e}^{2} \\  & ={e}^{2}+{e}^{14}.\end{aligned}
$$

So, the position of the particle at $t=5$ is $x={e}^{2}+{e}^{14}.$

canonical_examples.problem: A particle $P$ moves along the $x$-axis and its velocity at time $t$ is given by $v(t) = 2t + 3t^2.$ What is the total displacement of the particle between $t=1$ and $t=3?$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
We find the total displacement by calculating the definite integral of the velocity.

Let $d$ be the total displacement. Then, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}d & ={\int }_{1}^{3}(2t+3{t}^{2})\,\text{d}t \\  & ={({t}^{2}+{t}^{3})|}_{1}^{3} \\  & =[{3}^{2}+{3}^{3}]-[{1}^{2}+{1}^{3}] \\  & =[9+27]-[1+1] \\  & =36-2 \\  & =34.\end{aligned}
$$

So the total displacement between $t=1$ and $t=3$ is $34.$
